title: ⚖️ Eryndor Living Atlas VII — Slavery, Bondage, Serfdom & Resistance
rawNotionMarkup: New creator-directed worldbuilding for Eryndor, Year 3,847: slavery, bondage, serfdom and coercive labor exist as serious and distinct institutions. This material is a newly authored expansion, not recovered original campaign history. Names, proposed laws, affected populations, institutions and routes are all creator-revisable until reconciled with more source material. The five continents, existing political powers and living-world rules remain intact. No in-world time passes by writing this chapter; Gloin is still at Hadrik's archive desk on Autumn Day 22, \~11:25 AM. ## Creator correction — slavery is cross-species AND within a species Binding clarification: The example of an Urakai warlord taking Khazari miners is one possible scenario among innumerable others, not a central template or an ethnic assignment. Any established intelligent people can contain enslavers, enslaved people, liberators, indifferent bystanders and governments divided on the issue. Members of the same species can enslave each other, and members of different species can do so. A Khazari lord might exploit other Khazari laborers; human nobles might own human workers; an Urakai captain might enslave captured Urakai from a rival clan; a Goblin broker might prey on Goblin migrants; a mixed-species pirate crew might raid a mixed settlement. These are illustrations, not established atrocities or universal cultural practices. Motives are numerous and overlapping: mining or industrial expertise; agricultural and domestic labor; prestige and aristocratic power; military conquest; revenge and feuds; ransom and hostage-taking; debt collection; punishment; political control; territorial dispossession; discriminatory law; resource extraction; piracy; private enrichment; or opportunistic criminals exploiting weak law enforcement. Some traffickers target a skilled occupation, some target the vulnerable, and some have no coherent motive beyond profit and power. Species-specific strengths may influence an exploiter's choices, but never make enslavement biologically ordained or require all Khazari to be miners, all Urakai to be raiders, or all Goblins to be criminals. Regional governance matters more than ancestry: Practices differ between a city and its hinterland, noble houses and their towns, rival clans of the same people, independent Khazari Thrones, different southern sultanates and even two neighboring ships. Not every regime legalizes the same conduct; covert crimes can occur under prohibitions. Slavery may be multigenerational, systematic and economically consequential without every place being dominated by slavers. Story-design restraint: Avoid reflexively pairing one named species as “enslaver” and another as “victim.” Vary power relations based on local history, real institutions, military opportunities and individual actions. The Urakai–Khazari miner-raid example below is a single hypothetical example, not a preset actual raid, and the existing unidentified Urakai warlord from the original campaign is not automatically responsible. Any proposed faction named below is one faction among many; no monopoly. ## Grimdark directive — active enslavers, captive markets and predatory warlords Creator direction: Eryndor includes real, active enslavers, not merely abstract legal systems. Raiding warbands, traffickers, slaveholding lords, coerced-labor mine operators, pirates, corrupt officials and mercenary captains can capture people, separate families, sell captives, and enforce brutal labor. Some realms openly legalize the institution; others punish it; some officials quietly profit despite prohibitions. It is a major structural horror of parts of the world, not an occasional offscreen footnote. Case explicitly raised by the creator — Urakai warlord and Khazari mining captives: A particular Urakai warlord might assault an outlying Khazari mining village, murder or drive off defenders, seize surviving skilled miners and engineers, and force those captives into mines, quarry works, underground fortifications or mineral extraction. The desired labor expertise is the motive. Such raids could target Khazari surveyors, tunnel engineers, ventilation experts and smiths because a warlord wants industrial capacity without bargaining for skilled paid workers. Some families could be ransomed; other captives held, traded or forced to work. Free Khazari communities could fortify passes, pursue rescue missions, demand diplomatic responses and remember losses for generations. Hard distinction: This is an explicitly approved type of event, not an event that has already occurred in the current campaign. Do not assert that the unnamed warlord reported consolidating Urakai clans is this enslaver, that any specifically named Khazari hamlet was raided, or that the event is connected to the sealed eastern mine, Veyron, the First Throne or Gloin's ancestry. An Urakai raider can be a calculating slaver and an Urakai city can also be a sophisticated opponent of enslavement. Neither identity cancels the other. Urakai intelligence, universities and industry remain canon; culture and individual political choices explain war crimes rather than inherent biology. ### New proposed enslaver groups and their regional roles (Year 3,847 setting expansion) | New faction | Base and nature | Power and consequences | | --- | --- | --- | | Red Chain Bands | Sahradi plateau and oasis margins; raiders and slave traders | Attack exposed farms, convoys and settlements, supported by some corrupt brokers and opposed by local patrols and threatened communities | | Sable Yoke Houses | A minority of northern Sahradi estate courts and captive-labor markets | Powerful landowners treat captive workers as assets in agricultural estates and households; political allies resist emancipation | | Ash Collar Contractors | Valtorian frontier roads, quarries and military construction | Public-private penal and captive labor networks; some officials contest fraudulent convictions and brutal conditions | | Saltwake Reavers | Shattered Isles and sea approaches | Pirates and slavers who take crews or coastal inhabitants captive; maritime authorities and Merfolk polities resist them | | Black Fen Collectors | Orundel river margins | Fraudulent debt enforcers and kidnappers operating around disputed frontier jurisdictions | | Frost-Iron Captains | Tharvorn disputed passes | Ruthless border warbands who seize people for ransom or compelled labor during feuds; not representative of all northern people | | Iron-Tusk Reavers | Some Urakai frontier warbands on eastern Avarra, beyond established civil ports | A proposed example of a warlord-led band willing to enslave captured Khazari miners and engineers for industrial and fortress works. No established link to the unnamed major warlord from the campaign-opening news | | Hooked Ledger Network | Cross-border criminal intermediaries | Fraudulent employment documents and corrupt brokerage can allow enslavers to profit even in anti-slavery jurisdictions; no global mastermind is assumed | Provenance: The existence of enslavers and the mining-village Urakai warlord example are the creator's direction. All group names, precise territories, leaders, targets and schemes in this table are new provisional designs. They can be developed in play, replaced or retconned. This is not an exhaustive roster; local individual slavers or illegal captor gangs need not join a named organization. ### Why slavery can sustain elites but not make a kingdom economically efficient Captive miners, field workers, craftsmen and domestic servants may be used as inputs for iron, grain, canal and fortress systems, generating profit and coercive political power for owners. Yet guards, food, injury, sickness, escapes, low morale, hidden sabotage, resistance and war damage impose high costs. A realm can become politically dependent on the institution without slavery being inevitable or economically superior to free skilled labor. Khazari technical proficiency does not guarantee that an enslaver can simply force safe engineering; disastrous collapses, degraded work and escape attempts are plausible. ### Actual lived stakes and agency Captives remain people: injured workers, parents separated from children, welders and physicians, miners, teachers, farmers, couriers and warriors. Their fear, survival decisions, solidarity, escape and resistance have consequence. Raids can kill defenders, destroy food stores and uproot hamlets. Royal courts may respond with war, diplomacy, ransom, rescue, indifference or collusion, depending on actual institutions and public pressure. Abolitionists, escaped workers and local people can be brave, compromised, divided or frightened; Gloin is free to choose involvement, avoidance or another direction. Play principle: This is partially grimdark fantasy. Serious harm, murder, forced labor and betrayal can occur, alongside comedy, warm friendships, beauty and ordinary livelihoods. Don't sanitize atrocity into mere bureaucracy and don't sensationalize every scene. Don't impose an atrocity in every village, or predetermine attacks before game time passes. Keep culpability individual, legal status territorial, evidence distinct from rumour, and the consequences persistent. ## Foundational design: not every kingdom works this way, but some are deeply dependent The creator wants an unsanitized fantasy world. Outright slavery, hereditary servitude, debt bondage, war-captive labor, exploitative indenture, serfdom and penal labor exist in different legal forms in different parts of Eryndor. Some governments and landowners have built their wealth and institutions around unfree labor. Others prohibit enslavement, tolerate exploitative employment, protect fugitives or inconsistently enforce laws. A kingdom does not inherently need slavery to exist, but a particular aristocracy, export crop sector, mine, military frontier or royal treasury may have become dependent on it. That dependency creates genuine political and economic resistance to abolition. Ethical and species guardrail: A person is not inherently eligible to be enslaved because they are a Goblin, Ogre, Harpy, Urakai, Human or any other species. Captivity arises from law, power, war, prejudice, debt, criminality and historical circumstance. Targeting of certain communities may exist as discriminatory policy, but must be attributed to specific regimes and challenged in-world, not enshrined as biological truth. Enslaved people remain fully realized individuals with choices, dignity, skills, relationships, belief, fear, agency and histories. Depict exploitation soberly; no fetishization or gratuitous cruelty. ## Seven distinct institutions and legal questions | System | Status of the people affected | Sources of coercion | Distinction that matters | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Chattel slavery | Under a regime's law, people are property capable of being bought or sold | Capture, trade, legal purchase, forced sale | A person is treated as a transferable asset; lifetime captivity possible | | Hereditary servitude | Law attempts to assign unfree status by parentage | Birth registration, estate law, restricted family freedom | Not every jurisdiction accepts inheriting this status; rescue and legal status of children are contentious | | Debt bondage | Worker or family bound by claimed debt and fees | Manipulated ledgers, crop failures, emergency borrowing, court judgments | Debt may be perpetually extended; a supposedly voluntary agreement can be coercive | | Serfdom / tied tenancy | Farmer attached to estate or district with obligatory dues | Land tenure, lordly courts, movement restrictions | Unlike chattel slavery, the farmer is not necessarily owned and sold separately; rights vary | | Penal labor | Convicted prisoners compelled to work | Court sentence, wartime decree, corrupt judges | Can be finite with hearings, or a pretext for indefinite exploitation | | War-captive labor | Captives from wars or raids held under camp/custom laws | Military force, ransom and prisoner markets | Some polities permit prisoner exchanges or mandatory release; others convert captivity into lifelong slavery | | Indenture and corvée | Contract or state law obliges a period of labor | Migration passage debts, tax obligations, state works drafts | Some contracts have real end dates and protections; others conceal captivity | Magical coercion is a different and unusually alarming category: Where rare magic affects consent, memory, compulsion or movement, it can underpin unlawful confinement or abusive institutions; magical control is not an inexpensive universal slave-collar technology, and the lost art of Natural Magic harmonisation is not declared to be a technology for enslavement. Capabilities, risks and legality must be established under the existing magic system before use. ## Newly designed jurisdictional patchwork All laws and arrangements below are NEW proposed canon for Year 3,847, not earlier established legal codes. ### Avarra: independent Khazari Thrones - Karak-Varn: Legal ownership of a person is prohibited within royal jurisdiction in this new design. Licensed service contracts, guild apprenticeships, criminal sentencing and public-works duties exist; wage coercion, fraudulent apprenticeship fees and prison labor remain live concerns. This does not make Karak-Varn incorruptible. A smuggling ring might attempt to hide captives among freight. An accusation requires evidence, not automatic attribution to Edrik Voss, Veyron or the Royal Mining Office. - Seven independent Thrones: There is no single blanket Khazari law. New working differences: Az-Rhumen restricts debt attachment and protects audited wages; Thar-Keld uses harsh seasonal road-service obligations; Durn-Khaz permits limited court-ordered mining sentences; Karak-Orun tolerates bonded border work under disputed permits; Morn-Tar's salt/freight system includes debt-bound contract labor; Vuldur-Kaz imposes compulsory public furnace/levee duty in emergencies. These differences create actual borders, legal appeals and inter-Throne disputes. None proves that the Six Thrones secretly practice full chattel slavery. - Deepways: A freight master can carry legal goods through one Throne and commit a crime at the next gate by attempting to transport captives. Different courts argue over jurisdiction, debt documents and rescue. Human trafficking is dangerous and profitable for some criminals, but not an ordinary commodity accepted everywhere. ### Avarra: human monarchies, the merchant coast and Urakai societies - Aldermere: Some noble estates retain serfdom and binding manorial dues, while chartered towns, freemen, Halfling cooperatives and independent farmers have other legal statuses. Some lords advocate reform; others fear losing harvest labor. Free rural families can also be poor without being enslaved. - Valtorian Empire: A state-authorized frontier labor and prison-work system supplies military roads, quarries, irrigation and fortifications, with a mix of convicted offenders, coerced debtors and some war captives. Its military-administration interests can protect the system and falsify accounts. This is a proposed economic reliance in selected frontier districts, not an assertion that every imperial citizen is enslaved or that Valtoria's current mobilization automatically involves captive labor. - Shattered Coast Merchant Republics: Several coastal charters formally prohibit selling people, yet illegal trafficking, ransom markets, coercive ship service and debt-ship contracts continue under corrupt brokers or pirates. Neighboring republics disagree about extradition and freedom gained on reaching their ports. - Eastern Urakai confederations: Legal traditions differ by clan and city: some recognise limited-term war-captive service or ransom, others prohibit holding civilians captive, others allow harsh customary debt obligations. Scholars, clan elders and mixed city councils dispute these practices. No equation of Urakai with slaveholding by species or of their unidentified new warlord with a trafficking ring. ### Other continents - Sahrad: Some newly designed Southern Sultanate courts and oasis principalities legally recognise household, estate and plantation-like chattel or hereditary servitude alongside thriving free craftspeople, scholars, wage laborers and merchants. Other sultanates actively prohibit the trade and provide court protections to escaped captives. No single Sultanate law governs the entire continent; no religion or whole ethnic group is declared pro-slavery. Water rights, date estates, canal work, wealthy households and caravan markets make the political economy specific rather than generic. - Orundel: River federations may use compulsory tax labor for canals and levees, and some steppe confederations take captives during warfare, but several river councils reject sale of persons. Fraudulent debt contracts can move across ports. The vast continent is not one legal jurisdiction. - Tharvorn: Certain harsh frontier chiefs have temporary war-captive obligations and debt-bound households, disputed by fjord assemblies. Winter survival and fishing are labor-intensive, but not every winter village is a slave camp. - Vaelora: Some Crownwall estates or lake districts maintain land-tied obligations; other towns have strong antislavery charters and refuge laws. Ent councils, Eldar communities, Goblin charter towns and human lake ports have their own legal rights and disagreements. - Letharion and independent Eldar houses: The new design prohibits sale or ownership of persons in the royal heartwood realm, but long-lived apprenticeship agreements, guardianship and forest-service obligations can still be abused. Letharion is not automatically a universal emancipator, and Eldar diaspora elsewhere live under local law. - Merfolk polities: Some maritime jurisdictions ban captivity and enforce sanctuary; a minority may permit debt-bound reef labor or captive exchange. Underwater slavery cannot be assumed to be an ordinary surface-port business; the sea has independent authorities and treaty law. ## Economics — why some political elites defend coercion Coerced labor is not free. Owners, states and landholders still pay for food, guards, housing, tools, medicine (sometimes inadequately), transport, court bribes, punitive enforcement and capital. Productivity, flight, resistance, sabotage and deterioration reduce the value captured. A mine owner may favor forced labor because the legal framework lets them transfer costs and risks to captive workers, not because coercion is objectively the most efficient technique. | Sector | Why coercive labor might appear | Wider economy and conflict | | --- | --- | --- | | Great estates, grain and dates | Landed families use hereditary labor or tied tenants to control production | Peasant resistance, credit bondage, bad harvests, labour reform and food prices | | Mining, quarries and saltworks | Courts sentence workers, owners obtain debt-bound gangs or war captives | High fatalities, tunnel safety disputes, forged contracts, hired free-labor competition | | Fortifications, canals and roads | States impose work duties or use prisoners/war captives | Infrastructure may depend on coercion; legitimacy, taxes and public consent suffer | | Households and elite courts | Status, prestige, domestic work and rigid social hierarchy | Inheritance, family separation, emancipation disputes and service workers' rights | | Ships, caravans and ports | Captivity through piracy, manipulated passage debt or forced crews | Maritime law, rescue, harbor inspections, insurance and reputational costs | | Workshops and proto-industry | Bonded apprenticeships, prison labor or underpaid contractors | Guild resistance, quality problems, wage competition, industrial action | Abolition consequences: Freeing workers need not crash a whole kingdom. There can be expensive transitions, restitution disputes, new wage markets, loss of noble privilege, migration, bankrupt estates, paid labor shortages, political violence and new opportunities. Abolitionist movements may be mixed in aims, tactics and class. An owner claiming the economy “cannot survive without slavery” expresses a political interest, not necessarily economic truth. ### Suggested model variables for any jurisdiction (GM-only, no fake precision) - Legal status classes and who can lawfully own, hire, arrest, ransom or free a captive. - Proportion of the workforce coerced by specific region/sector, not an invented universal world percentage. - Annual output dependent on coerced labor, the state's taxes/fees from that sector, and free-labor alternatives. - Food, shelter, guarding and medical costs; deaths and births; flight risk; liberation, manumission, marriage and children’s status; actual enforcement resources. - Court appeal rights, language barriers, record forgery, nationality, cross-border extradition and protections from abuse. - Family and community networks, religious/legal opposition, solidarity and organised resistance by those held in bondage. - Trade price shocks, contract fraud, military raids and civil protest, with cause and calendar tracked as game time advances. Population accounting: Enslaved people, serfs, bonded laborers and other captives are already included in each resident species' numerical total in the Atlas population tables. Do not add a second “slave population” and double-count them. No exact global count of captive people has been established yet. Future estimates should be built from regional law, sector capacity and migration, and must distinguish reported census from actual conditions. ## People's lives — the institution is not a backdrop prop - The enslaved person may be a skilled smith, a retired soldier, a child’s parent, a scholar, an excellent navigator, a farmer, a patient, a spouse, a rebel or someone hoping simply to survive. They have relationships and agency beyond their condition. - Different individuals respond differently: cooperation for safety, secrecy, legal petition, self-purchase where lawful, strike, revolt, escape, diplomacy, sabotage or quiet endurance. No one response is prescribed as morally or narratively compulsory. - Free neighbors can support, profit from, condemn, ignore or challenge the system. Officials disagree; some laws are unenforced, some courts are bribed, and others issue meaningful remedies. - Graphic violence, sexual coercion and abuses may be part of historical allegations or background consequences, but need not be described in lurid detail for the world to feel grim. The important facts are human experiences, institutions, consequences and the decisions people face. - No plot requires Gloin to rescue every person he sees or become an abolitionist. But he cannot assume being a neutral buyer, guard or caravan passenger has no consequences. ## Illustrative newly designed locations and conflicts Valtoria — Northwatch: A frontier contractor's prison labor crew quarrels with a free masonry guild about wages and working conditions. Some prisoners have legitimate sentences; others were convicted under questionable paperwork. A magistrate may have enough power to examine records but must survive political pressure. This conflict is not established as an event already experienced by Gloin. Aldermere — Greenbarley hinterland: An estate lord threatens to remove tied farming families from a field unless they increase customary dues after a bad harvest. A miller, local abbey and cooperative offer conflicting interpretations of tenure law. Sahrad — Thirty Wells caravan junction: A broker attempts to seize a household for a fabricated debt. The oasis magistrate and visiting merchants disagree over documentation. Another principality's emancipation edict may apply if the family crosses a border; the crossing itself is risky and not guaranteed. Shattered Isles — Nacre Key: A merchant sea captain attempts to exchange captured sailors for goods while describing them as 'contract passengers.' Harbor officials and Merfolk witnesses have standing to contest that fiction under some jurisdictions' law. Deepways — contested toll office: A convoy transport manifest conceals a bound group, raising disputes between independent Thronal jurisdictions. The involvement of any named officer from Gloin's current case must not be invented. Bramblebridge: Its new Free Hearth Charter protects local residents' legal standing, but a traveler might arrive with alleged debt claims from another jurisdiction. A lively mixed-species town must decide what its own courts can enforce, and a scared person may need time to prove identity. This need not become the plot of every visit. ## Gameplay and provenance rules - Knowledge is limited: Gloin does not know every kingdom's legal structure, hidden trafficking route, captive registry or abuse. He learns through travel, law, testimony, records and rumors; rumours may be false. - No retroactive guilt: No part of the active First Throne/eastern mine investigation, Veyron's office, Edrik Voss's conduct, Maela's research or Hadrik's archive records is automatically linked to slavery by authorial convenience. - Meaningful player options: A player may seek lawful work, inform authorities, support emancipation, escort refugees, refuse a contract, negotiate manumission, investigate a debt ledger, join a caravan, free captives in conflict, ignore a report or leave a region. Consequences depend on state power and what actually happens. - No predetermined uprisings or atrocities: A potential background injustice is not a secretly scheduled bloodbath. Offscreen developments advance only with the campaign clock; past scenes remain unchanged unless the creator explicitly retcons. - Source status: Slavery’s presence in Eryndor is newly established by creator direction. The detailed models and jurisdictional examples in this chapter are new provisional worldbuilding, not claims of prior dialogue. Every model rule and proposed law is subject to creator revision; existing political canon supersedes accidental conflict.
